body.html: The great vessels leave and enter the heart in the middle mediastinum and pass through the superior mediastinum (behind the manubrium, in front of T1-T4; above the plane through the sternal angle and the T4-T5 disc). From front to back it contains the thymus, the brachiocephalic veins and superior vena cava, the aortic arch and its branches, the trachea, the oesophagus and thoracic duct, plus the phrenic and vagus nerves and the left recurrent laryngeal nerve.

Pulmonary trunk: from the conus arteriosus of the right ventricle, in a common pericardial sheath with the ascending aorta; divides at the T5-T6 level (behind the 3rd left costal cartilage) into the right pulmonary artery (behind the ascending aorta and SVC) and left pulmonary artery (below the arch, in front of the descending aorta). Ascending aorta: from the left ventricle (aortic orifice at the lower edge of the 3rd left costal cartilage) up to the 2nd right costal cartilage, where it becomes the arch; just above the valve are three aortic sinuses; the right and left coronary arteries arise from the right and left sinuses. The lower half of the SVC, a short segment of the IVC (after crossing the diaphragm at T8) and the pulmonary veins (usually two from each lung, into the left atrium) lie inside the pericardial sac.

Thymus: most anterior, behind the manubrium; large in children, atrophies after puberty to fat; supplied by internal thoracic artery branches; common site of ectopic parathyroid glands (same third pharyngeal pouch origin). Brachiocephalic veins: each formed by the internal jugular + subclavian veins behind the clavicle's medial end; the left crosses to the right behind the manubrium (above it in children, less protected) to join the right and form the SVC behind the 1st right costal cartilage. The SVC ends in the right atrium at the 3rd right costal cartilage, receives the azygos vein, and forms the right superolateral mediastinal border on X-ray. The left superior intercostal vein drains spaces 2-4 over the arch into the left brachiocephalic vein. Aortic arch: begins and ends at the sternal angle level; branches: brachiocephalic trunk (→ right subclavian and right common carotid), left common carotid, left subclavian. The descending thoracic aorta continues in the posterior mediastinum to the aortic hiatus (T12). Clinical: SVC and IVC lie on one vertical axis, so catheters can pass from the neck to the IVC (transjugular liver biopsy, TIPS, IVC filters for deep vein thrombosis).

A section through the middle of the arm shows anterior and posterior compartments separated by the medial and lateral intermuscular septa attached to the humerus. The brachial canal on the medial side carries the main vessels and nerves.

Anterior (flexors, musculocutaneous nerve): brachialis (deep; humeral shaft → coronoid process of the ulna; pure elbow flexor), biceps brachii (superficial; short head from the coracoid, long head from the supraglenoid tubercle → radial tuberosity; elbow flexion and supination), coracobrachialis (coracoid → medial humerus; flexes the arm). Posterior: triceps brachii: long head (infraglenoid tubercle), lateral head (above the radial groove), medial head (below it) → olecranon; elbow extension; radial nerve. The radial nerve and deep brachial artery (profunda brachii) run in the radial groove.

On the medial side, in front of the medial septum, it contains the brachial artery with two brachial veins, the median nerve and the ulnar nerve. The brachial artery continues the axillary artery at the lower border of pectoralis major and divides at the elbow into the radial and ulnar arteries; branches: muscular, profunda brachii (into the radial groove), superior and inferior ulnar collateral arteries. The median nerve travels with the artery, ending medial to it at the elbow. The ulnar nerve is medial and, in the distal third, passes behind the medial intermuscular septum toward the back of the medial epicondyle.

The cubital fold is the set of structures in front of the elbow, bounded by horizontal lines about 4 cm above and below the joint line and vertical lines through the two epicondyles. It contains three muscle groups, two grooves carrying vessels and nerves, and the superficial veins used for blood tests.

Medial epicondylar muscles (from the medial epicondyle; lateral to medial): pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus, flexor carpi ulnaris. Lateral epicondylar muscles: brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis. Median group: the biceps tendon (radial tuberosity) and brachialis (proximal ulna, coronoid process). Medial bicipital groove (between the medial muscles and the median group, closed by the bicipital aponeurosis): brachial artery with two veins, dividing about 2 cm below the joint line into radial and ulnar arteries, and the median nerve. Lateral bicipital groove (between lateral muscles and median group): the radial nerve, dividing into an anterior sensory branch and a posterior motor branch that pierces the supinator to supply all posterior forearm muscles.

The brachial pulse is felt in the medial bicipital groove. The superficial veins form an 'M' network, continuing as the cephalic vein laterally and the basilic vein medially, used for injections, blood sampling and IV infusions. After any elbow trauma, systematically check the brachial artery, median, radial and ulnar nerves (the ulnar passes behind, in the epicondylo-olecranon groove).

A section through the middle third of the forearm shows three muscular compartments: anterior (flexors and pronators, with the median and ulnar nerves and the radial and ulnar arteries), lateral and posterior (extensors, radial nerve).

Four layers. Layer 1 (epitrochlear, from the medial epicondyle; lateral to medial): pronator teres (→ lateral radius; pronation; median n.), flexor carpi radialis (→ base of 2nd metacarpal; wrist flexion), palmaris longus (→ palmar aponeurosis), flexor carpi ulnaris (→ pisiform; ulnar n.). Layer 2: flexor digitorum superficialis (medial epicondyle, ulna, radius; its arch covers the median nerve) → sides of the middle phalanges of fingers 2-5; flexes the middle phalanx. Layer 3: flexor pollicis longus (anterior radius → distal phalanx of the thumb) and flexor digitorum profundus (anterior ulna → distal phalanges of fingers 2-5; median n. for fingers 2-3, ulnar n. for fingers 4-5). Layer 4: supinator (lateral epicondyle → proximal radius; supination; deep radial n.) and pronator quadratus (distal radius ↔ ulna; median n.).

Median nerve: passes under the arch of FDS and supplies all anterior muscles except flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of FDP. Ulnar nerve: from the epicondylo-olecranon groove, runs under flexor carpi ulnaris; supplies FCU and the medial half of FDP. Radial and ulnar arteries arise ~2 cm below the elbow joint line, each with two venae comitantes. The radial artery runs under brachioradialis, then superficially in the pulse groove between the flexor carpi radialis (medially) and brachioradialis (laterally) tendons: where the radial pulse is taken.

Lateral (radial nerve): brachioradialis (lateral supracondylar humerus → radial styloid; elbow flexion), extensor carpi radialis longus (→ base of 2nd metacarpal) and brevis (→ base of 3rd metacarpal): wrist extension. Posterior (deep branch of radial nerve): superficial layer: anconeus (elbow extension), extensor digitorum (four tendons; central slip → middle phalanx, lateral slips → distal phalanx), extensor digiti minimi, extensor carpi ulnaris (→ base of 5th metacarpal); deep layer: abductor pollicis longus (→ base of 1st metacarpal), extensor pollicis brevis (→ proximal phalanx of thumb), extensor pollicis longus (→ distal phalanx of thumb), extensor indicis.

The palm has three compartments: thenar (thumb muscles), hypothenar (little-finger muscles) and middle palmar (finger flexor tendons and interosseous muscles). Knowing their nerve supply explains the classic hand deformities of median and ulnar nerve injuries.

Thenar (superficial to deep): abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, flexor pollicis brevis, adductor pollicis. Supplied by the thenar (recurrent) branch of the median nerve, except the adductor pollicis and the deep head of flexor pollicis brevis, supplied by the ulnar nerve. Hypothenar (superficial to deep): palmaris brevis, abductor digiti minimi, flexor digiti minimi, opponens digiti minimi: all supplied by the ulnar nerve.

Contains the flexor tendons of the fingers and the interosseous muscles, which arise from the sides of the metacarpals. The dorsal interossei abduct the fingers (spread them) and the palmar interossei adduct them (bring them together): the mnemonics 'DAB' and 'PAD'. All interossei are supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
The hand is supplied by the radial and ulnar arteries, joined by two palmar arches, and innervated in the palm by the median and ulnar nerves, which pass through the carpal tunnel and Guyon's canal.

Radial artery: at the wrist runs in the pulse groove between the brachioradialis (lateral) and flexor carpi radialis (medial) tendons, gives the radiopalmar (superficial palmar) branch, passes through the floor of the anatomical snuffbox to the back of the hand, then returns to the palm through the first web space. Ulnar artery: medially, lateral to the pisiform, stays anterior and gives the ulnopalmar (deep palmar) branch. Superficial palmar arch: ulnar artery + radiopalmar branch, in front of the flexor tendons, with the branches of the median nerve. Deep palmar arch: radial artery + ulnopalmar branch, behind the flexor tendons. The arches give interdigital arteries that divide above the web spaces into the digital collateral arteries.

Median nerve: passes through the carpal tunnel (carpal bones behind, flexor retinaculum in front) with the finger flexor tendons; gives the thenar branch (abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis) and interdigital nerves to the 1st-3rd spaces. Sensory: palmar surface and pulp of the thumb, index, middle and lateral half of the ring finger. Ulnar nerve: medial, lateral to the pisiform, with the ulnar artery, through Guyon's canal. Deep branch: all interossei, adductor pollicis and the hypothenar muscles. Superficial branches: 4th interdigital space and medial side of the 5th finger. Sensory: medial half of the ring finger and the whole little finger (palmar side).

The heart lies in the middle mediastinum, inside the pericardium, between T4 and T8. It is a four-chambered muscular pump: thin-walled atria receive blood at low pressure; thick-walled ventricles pump it through the pulmonary and systemic circuits.

Layers: epicardium (visceral pericardium), myocardium (contractile muscle), endocardium (endothelium lining the chambers). Cone shape: the base faces posteriorly (mainly the left atrium with the pulmonary veins, toward T6-T9, separated by the pericardium, oesophagus and aorta); sternocostal and diaphragmatic surfaces; apex. Borders: superior (auricles, ascending aorta, pulmonary trunk, SVC entry), inferior (right ventricle), left (left ventricle and left auricle), right (SVC, right atrium, IVC). Sulci: sulcus terminalis (outside the right atrium; crista terminalis inside), coronary (AV) sulcus (right and left coronary, circumflex arteries, coronary sinus), anterior interventricular groove (LAD and great cardiac vein), posterior interventricular groove (posterior interventricular artery and middle cardiac vein).

Parietal pericardium = outer fibrous layer + inner serous layer; the visceral pericardium (epicardium) covers the heart; the pericardial space lies between the serous layers. Sinuses: transverse (behind the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk, in front of the left atrium and pulmonary veins) and oblique (behind the heart, bounded by the reflections around the pulmonary veins and IVC).

Right atrium: receives SVC, IVC and the coronary sinus; auricle with pectinate muscles; smooth sinus venarum; outflow via the tricuspid valve. Right ventricle: most of the anterior surface; trabeculae carneae, papillary muscles with chordae tendineae preventing cusp prolapse, and the moderator band (septomarginal trabecula); outflow through the pulmonary valve. Left atrium: most of the base, touches the oesophagus, receives four pulmonary veins; outflow through the mitral (bicuspid) valve. Left ventricle: long, conical, much thicker wall; outflow through the aortic valve. Left coronary artery (above the left aortic cusp; short but supplies more myocardium: most of the LV, LA, bundle of His, anterior septum) → LAD (anterior LV, apex, anterior septum) and circumflex (posterolateral LV, marginal branches). Right coronary artery (above the right cusp, in the right AV groove): right atrium and ventricle, SA and AV nodes; gives the posterior descending artery (inferior wall, posterior septum) in most people. Conduction: SA node → AV node → bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibres.

Anatomy (Greek anatome, 'cutting up'; Latin equivalent: dissection), also called morphology, is the study of the structure of the human body from the macroscopic to the microscopic level. It is the basis of physiology, clinical practice, surgery and medical imaging. Levels of organisation: chemical (atoms, macromolecules) → cellular → tissue (epithelial, connective, muscle, nervous) → organ (lung, liver, brain) → organ system → organism.

Gross anatomy: structures visible to the naked eye, studied by dissection; includes surface anatomy (landmarks, abdominal quadrants), regional anatomy (the basis of surgery) and systemic anatomy (organs grouped by system). Microscopic anatomy (histology): cells, tissues, fine structure of organs. Developmental anatomy (embryology): how structures form, from fertilisation to adulthood. Pathological anatomy: structural changes caused by disease (cancer, inflammation). Radiographic anatomy: structure seen by imaging: X-rays pass easily through air and fat (radiotransparent) but are absorbed by bone, calcium stones and metals (radiopaque); CT rotates a narrow beam around the patient and a computer builds cross-sections; MRI uses electromagnetic energy for multiplanar sections. The official vocabulary is the Terminologia Anatomica (which replaced the Nomina Anatomica); names come from objects (lunate, pisiform, scaphoid, mitral valve, coronary), geometric shapes (trapezius, pyramidalis, quadratus), colours (grey and white matter, yellow ligament).

Anatomical position: standing erect, feet flat and toes forward, eyes forward, palms facing anteriorly with thumbs pointing away from the body. Clinical positions: supine (face up), prone (face down), right lateral recumbent (lying on the right side: access to the left side) and left lateral recumbent. Regions: axial (head, neck, trunk: thorax, abdomen, pelvis, perineum) and appendicular (upper and lower limbs). Terms: superior (cranial) vs inferior (caudal); supra vs infra (supraspinatus above, infraspinatus below the scapular spine); medial (internal) vs lateral (external); anterior (ventral) vs posterior (dorsal) ('dorsal' also names the back of the hand and top of the foot); superficial vs deep; proximal vs distal, reserved for the limbs (near or far from the limb root). The hand's axis passes through the 3rd finger, the foot's through the 2nd toe.

Planes: sagittal (median = equal halves; parasagittal = unequal), frontal (coronal): anterior/posterior, transverse (horizontal): superior/inferior (axial CT/MRI slices). Axes: left-right (flexion/extension, e.g. hip, knee), anteroposterior (abduction/adduction, e.g. shoulder), vertical (rotation, e.g. neck). Shoulder (multiaxial ball-and-socket): flexion/extension, abduction/adduction, medial/lateral rotation. Elbow: uniaxial hinge (flexion/extension only). Forearm: pronation (palm turns backward) and supination (palm forward) at the radio-ulnar joints. Wrist: flexion/extension, radial and ulnar deviation. Fingers: abduction/adduction relative to the middle finger. Hip: flexion/extension in the sagittal plane (walking), abduction/adduction in the frontal plane.

The lungs, organs of gas exchange, lie on each side of the mediastinum in the pleural cavities, attached to the trachea and heart by their roots. The pulmonary circulation brings deoxygenated blood to the respiratory tissue (pulmonary arteries from the right ventricle; oxygenated blood returns in the pulmonary veins to the left atrium), while bronchial vessels nourish the non-respiratory tissue with oxygenated blood. Parasympathetic innervation causes bronchoconstriction.

The trachea runs from the larynx into the thorax and bifurcates into the right and left main bronchi at T4-T5. The right main bronchus gives three lobar (secondary) bronchi (superior, middle, inferior); the left gives two. Each lobar bronchus divides into segmental (tertiary) bronchi, then bronchioles ending in alveolar sacs.

Each lung is a half-cone with a base on the diaphragm, an apex rising above rib 1 into the neck (crossed in front by the subclavian artery and vein), a costal surface against the ribs, a mediastinal surface with the hilum, and three borders (sharp inferior and anterior, rounded posterior). Neighbouring structures (heart, great vessels, ribs) indent the lung surfaces. The root (main bronchus, pulmonary artery and veins, nerves, lymphatics) is sleeved by mediastinal pleura reflecting into visceral pleura; the outlined area is the hilum. Right lung: three lobes (superior, middle, inferior) separated by the oblique and horizontal fissures; shorter and wider because the right dome is higher, but slightly larger overall. Left lung: two lobes (superior, inferior) separated by the oblique fissure (along rib 6); instead of a middle lobe it has the cardiac notch and the lingula, an extension of the superior lobe.

The scapular region lies on the posterior, superolateral thorax. The palpable spine of the scapula runs obliquely up and out to end in the acromion. Its muscles are in two layers, and gaps between them transmit nerves and vessels to the arm.

Superficial: trapezius (external occipital protuberance, nuchal ligament, spines of T1-T12 → lateral third of clavicle, spine and acromion; elevates the shoulders and retracts the scapula; spinal accessory nerve, CN XI) and latissimus dorsi (spines T7-T12, thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest → bicipital groove of the humerus; adduction and medial rotation; thoracodorsal nerve). Deep: supraspinatus (supraspinous fossa → top of the greater tubercle; abduction; suprascapular nerve), infraspinatus (infraspinous fossa → greater tubercle; lateral rotation; suprascapular nerve), teres minor (lateral border → greater tubercle; lateral rotation; axillary nerve), teres major (inferior angle → humerus medial to latissimus; adduction and medial rotation; lower subscapular nerve), rhomboids (spines C4-T4 → medial border; retract the scapula; dorsal scapular nerve), levator scapulae (transverse processes C1-C4 → superomedial angle; elevates the scapula).

Between teres minor (above) and teres major (below), the long head of triceps divides the gap into the lateral quadrangular (humerotricipital) space, carrying the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery, and the medial triangular (omo-tricipital) space (circumflex scapular artery). Below teres major, the triangular interval (humerotricipital fissure) transmits the radial nerve. Deltoid: forms the rounded shoulder; clavicular (lateral third of clavicle), acromial and spinal parts → deltoid tuberosity; main abductor of the shoulder; supplied by the axillary nerve.

The shoulder joins the upper limb to the thorax: bounded above by the clavicle, below by the lower border of pectoralis major, medially by the midsternal line and laterally by the arm. It has an anterior region (medial pectoral region with the breast, lateral deltoid region) and a posterior (scapular) region. Surface anatomy: the deltopectoral groove between pectoral region and deltoid, with the coracoid process palpable at its top.

The axillary fossa is a quadrangular pyramid, the hilum of the upper limb for its vessels, nerves and lymphatics. Anterior wall: superficial pectoralis major (from medial clavicle, sternum and first six costal cartilages, rectus sheath → lateral lip of the bicipital groove; adduction and medial rotation; pectoral nerves); deep subclavius (clavicle → 1st rib; lowers clavicle, protects subclavian vessels) and pectoralis minor (ribs 3-5 → coracoid; lowers scapula, raises ribs), wrapped in the clavipectoral fascia, which forms the suspensory ligament of the axilla and is pierced by the cephalic vein and the thoracoacromial artery. Posterior wall: subscapularis (medial rotation; subscapular nerve) and the tendon of teres major. Medial wall: serratus anterior (medial border of scapula → first 8 ribs; protracts the scapula; long thoracic nerve). Lateral wall: coracobrachialis (flexes the arm; pierced by the musculocutaneous nerve, the nerve of elbow flexion) and the short head of biceps.

Axillary artery: continues the subclavian and becomes the brachial artery at the lower border of pectoralis major; five branches: thoracoacromial, superior thoracic, subscapular, inferior (lateral) thoracic, and the trunk of the anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries. The axillary vein lies medial to the artery, receives the matching veins and the cephalic vein, and continues as the subclavian vein. Brachial plexus cords around the artery: lateral cord → musculocutaneous nerve and lateral root of the median nerve; medial cord → medial root of the median, ulnar nerve, medial cutaneous nerves of arm and forearm; posterior cord → axillary (circumflex) nerve and radial nerve. Axillary lymph nodes drain the breast, the anterolateral chest wall and the upper limb: key in breast cancer staging.

The upper limb has five topographical regions: shoulder, arm, elbow, forearm and hand. Surface anatomy lets you locate bones, muscles, pulses and veins by sight and touch, and recognise deformities after trauma. This handout also describes the three main joints. It is a machine translation from French; the terms below are corrected.

Shoulder: the rounded 'stump' is the deltoid; above it the lateral clavicle and acromioclavicular joint. The clavicle separates the supraclavicular fossa from the pectoral region, which is divided from the deltoid by the deltopectoral groove (this disappears in shoulder dislocation). Behind, the spine of the scapula runs obliquely to the acromion, between the supraspinous and infraspinous fossae. Below (arm abducted), the axilla lies between the pectoralis major in front and latissimus dorsi behind. Elbow: in front, three projections (biceps in the middle, epicondylar muscle masses on each side) separated by the medial and lateral bicipital grooves; the brachial pulse is felt in the medial groove, and the thin skin shows the 'M' venous network, the preferred site for injections and blood tests. Behind, the olecranon and the two epicondyles form an isosceles triangle with the elbow flexed at 90° and a straight line in extension; this relationship is altered in elbow dislocation. Wrist: in front, the tendons of flexor carpi ulnaris (medial), palmaris longus and flexor carpi radialis, and brachioradialis (lateral); the radial pulse is felt in the groove between FCR and brachioradialis; behind, the ulnar head is prominent. Hand: palm with a central hollow, the convex thenar eminence and the smaller hypothenar eminence; the digitopalmar crease lies 10-15 mm below the MCP joint, the PIP crease is double and the DIP crease single. On the back, the anatomical snuffbox at the base of the thumb is bounded by extensor pollicis longus medially and extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus laterally.

A synovial joint has cartilage-covered surfaces, a capsule and ligaments, and a synovial membrane secreting synovial fluid (sometimes with fibrocartilage). Shoulder (scapulohumeral): humeral head and glenoid cavity deepened by the glenoid labrum; a very lax capsule reinforced in front by the coracohumeral and superior, middle and inferior glenohumeral ligaments; three degrees of freedom: flexion (antepulsion, 180°) and extension (retropulsion, 50°), abduction (180°) and adduction, internal and external rotation, combined in circumduction. Little bony interlocking and great mobility explain frequent dislocations, mostly anterior; X-rays show bones and joint space but not capsule, ligaments or cartilage. Elbow: three joints in one capsule: humero-ulnar (trochlea and trochlear notch), humeroradial (capitulum and radial head) and proximal radio-ulnar, reinforced by the medial and lateral collateral ligaments; one degree of freedom: flexion (about 130°) and extension; it also takes part in pronation-supination (about 180° in total) with the radio-ulnar joints. Wrist (radiocarpal): distal radius and the triangular fibrocartilage above the scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum; two degrees of freedom: flexion and extension (about 90° each) and radial (about 15°) and ulnar (about 45°) deviation.
The thoracic muscles move the upper limb and scapula, fill the intercostal spaces, and power breathing through the diaphragm, the principal muscle of respiration.

Anterior wall: pectoralis major (sternum, clavicle, costal margin → bicipital groove; flexes, adducts and medially rotates the humerus), pectoralis minor (ribs 3-5 → coracoid; stabilises the scapula), subclavius (clavicle ↔ rib 1; depresses the clavicle); all serve as accessory muscles of deep inspiration. Lateral wall: serratus anterior (ribs 1-8 → medial border of scapula; protracts and stabilises the scapula). Back: superficial (trapezius, levator scapulae, rhomboids, latissimus dorsi), intermediate (serratus posterior superior and inferior) and deep muscles.

Eleven intercostal spaces, each with three layers; the intercostal nerves and vessels run between the second and third layers. External intercostals (superficial; fibres downward and forward, from the rib tubercles to the costochondral joints, then the external intercostal membrane): raise the ribs → inspiration. Internal intercostals (middle; fibres at right angles, from the sternum to the rib angles, then the internal intercostal membrane): lower the ribs → expiration. Innermost intercostals (deepest, thin): probably help depress the ribs.

Separates thorax and abdomen; peripheral muscle converging on a central tendon; dome-shaped, descends (flattens) on contraction; the right dome (on the liver) is higher than the left (on the gastric fundus). Origins: lumbar (right crus from L1-L3, left crus from L1-L2), costal (inner surfaces of the lower six ribs), sternal (back of the xiphoid). Innervation: the phrenic nerves (C3, C4, C5), motor, and sensory to the central diaphragm, pericardium, mediastinal and diaphragmatic pleura; they run on the anterior scalene, enter between subclavian vein and artery, and descend in front of the lung roots between the mediastinal pleura and pericardium with the pericardiacophrenic vessels. Openings: caval (T8), in the central tendon right of midline: inferior vena cava; oesophageal (T10): oesophagus and vagal trunks; aortic (T12): aorta, thoracic duct (azygos vein).

The thoracic skeleton is the 12 thoracic vertebrae behind, the 12 pairs of ribs at the sides and the sternum with the costal cartilages in front. It protects the heart, lungs and great vessels and anchors the muscles that support the shoulder girdle and move the upper limbs. Landmarks: jugular notch, sternal angle (rib 2, T4-T5), xiphoid process (T9), costal margins (cartilages 7-10).

Three parts. Manubrium: jugular notch flanked by the sternoclavicular joints (the only bony link between upper limb and axial skeleton); receives rib 1. Sternal angle (of Louis): manubriosternal junction, a palpable ridge marking rib 2 (so all ribs can be counted), the T4-T5 level, the start and end of the aortic arch and the tracheal bifurcation. Body: articulates with costal cartilages 2-7 (demifacet for 2, facets for 3-6, demifacet for 7). Xiphoid process: smallest part, at T9, variable in shape, cartilaginous then ossified.

True ribs 1-7 attach directly to the sternum through their own cartilages; false ribs 8-10 join the cartilage above; floating ribs 11-12 have no anterior attachment. Ribs run obliquely downward from back to front (rib 2 meets T2 behind but the sternal angle at T4 in front), so an axial CT slice cuts several ribs. Typical ribs (2-10): head and neck (costovertebral joint with demifacets of adjacent vertebrae), tubercle (transverse process), shaft with a sharp lower border and the costal groove; the anterior end joins the costal cartilage. Fractures occur just anterior to the angle, the weakest point, and can tear the pleura (pneumothorax). Atypical ribs 1, 11, 12: rib 1 lies under the clavicle (not palpable) and bears the scalene tubercle (anterior scalene) with the groove for the subclavian vein in front and the subclavian artery behind.

Intercostal spaces hold three muscle layers. In the costal groove, between the inner two layers: vein (highest), artery, nerve (lowest): 'VAN'. The nerve is least protected; smaller collateral branches run along the upper border of the rib below.
7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar vertebrae, the sacrum (5 fused) and the coccyx (3-4 fused). Thoracic vertebrae carry costal facets on their bodies and transverse processes for the ribs.

The thorax is an irregular cylinder with a narrow superior thoracic aperture (open, continuous with the neck) and a wide inferior thoracic aperture closed by the diaphragm. Its cavity has three compartments: right and left pleural cavities (each around a lung) and the central mediastinum, which completely separates them and contains the heart, oesophagus, trachea, major nerves and great vessels. The pleural cavities extend above rib 1 into the neck.

Landmarks: clavicles (manubrium to acromion), jugular notch between their medial ends, sternal angle (of Louis) between manubrium and body, where rib 2 articulates, at the T4-T5 level. Vertical lines: midsternal, midclavicular (just medial to the nipple), anterior axillary (pectoralis major fold), midaxillary, posterior axillary (latissimus dorsi fold). The wall: 12 thoracic vertebrae and discs behind, 12 pairs of ribs with three layers of intercostal muscles laterally, the sternum and costal cartilages (mobility, elasticity) in front.

Superior aperture: body of T1, medial margins of the first ribs, and the manubrium (upper margin at the T2-T3 disc level); tilted forward; head and neck structures pass through it vertically, upper limb structures pass over rib 1. Inferior aperture: body of T12, rib 12 and the end of rib 11, cartilages of ribs 7-10 (costal margin), and the xiphoid process; the xiphisternal joint lies at the T9-T10 disc level; the posterior margin is lower than the anterior. The diaphragm arises radially from the margins and converges on a central tendon; it forms two domes, the right higher (up to rib 5, above the liver). The oesophagus and inferior vena cava pierce it; the aorta passes behind it. Contraction flattens the domes and enlarges the thorax.

The mediastinum runs from sternum to vertebrae and from the superior to the inferior aperture. A plane through the sternal angle and the T4-T5 disc divides it into superior and inferior parts; the inferior is split by the pericardium into anterior (sternum to pericardium), middle (pericardium and heart) and posterior (pericardium to vertebrae). Each pleural cavity is lined by pleura: parietal pleura on the walls, reflecting at the lung root (airway, pulmonary vessels, lymphatics, nerves) into visceral pleura on the lung, with only a potential space between them. The lungs do not fill the cavity completely, leaving recesses for expansion; the largest and clinically most important is the costodiaphragmatic recess, where fluid collects (pleural effusion).

The thoracic wall (vertebrae, ribs, sternum, intercostal muscles) is supplied by neurovascular bundles running in each intercostal space, anastomosing arteries from the subclavian artery and aorta, veins to the brachiocephalic and azygos systems, and lymph nodes that also drain the breast.

In each space the bundle runs in the costal groove of the upper rib, between the internal and innermost intercostals: vein, artery, nerve from top to bottom. Intercostal nerves are the ventral rami of T1-T11 (T12 = subcostal nerve), named by their space, giving lateral and anterior cutaneous (sensory) and muscular (motor) branches. Arteries: the internal thoracic artery (from the subclavian; inside the cage just lateral to the sternum) gives the anterior intercostal arteries and the anterior perforating arteries (pectoralis major, skin; the 2nd-4th give medial mammary branches) and ends as the musculophrenic (anterior intercostals of spaces 7-9, pierces the diaphragm) and superior epigastric arteries. Posterior intercostal arteries: the first two from the supreme intercostal artery (costocervical trunk), the rest from the thoracic aorta; they anastomose with the anterior ones. The subcostal artery runs below rib 12.

Internal thoracic vein → brachiocephalic vein. Anterior intercostal veins → musculophrenic and internal thoracic veins. Posterior intercostal veins: the upper two → brachiocephalic veins; the lower nine → azygos system → superior vena cava. Lymph nodes: parasternal (along the internal thoracic artery; medial breast, intercostal spaces, diaphragm, upper abdominal wall → junction of internal jugular and subclavian veins), intercostal (near rib heads; → cisterna chyli or thoracic duct), phrenic (on the diaphragm; pericardium, diaphragm, liver → mediastinal nodes).

Secretory glandular tissue, superficial fascia and skin in the pectoral region; the mammary gland overlies ribs 2 to 6, between the sternum and the midaxillary line, within the superficial fascia, surrounded by fat that determines size and shape; it enlarges during the menstrual cycle and pregnancy. It lies on the deep fascia of pectoralis major and serratus anterior, separated by the loose retromammary space, which gives it mobility. Lymph drains mainly to the axillary nodes laterally and the parasternal nodes medially.
The upper (thoracic) limb has four segments: shoulder, arm, forearm and hand. The shoulder (pectoral) girdle, made of the clavicle and scapula, connects it to the thorax.

Clavicle: long bone shaped like an italic 'S', joining the sternum (medially) to the acromion (laterally). Anterior border: pectoralis major (medial two-thirds) and deltoid (lateral third); posterior border: sternocleidomastoid (medially) and trapezius (laterally). Inferior surface: groove for subclavius, coracoclavicular (conoid and trapezoid) and costoclavicular ligaments.

Scapula: flat triangular bone on the posterolateral thorax. Anterior subscapular fossa (subscapularis). Posterior surface divided by the spine into supraspinous (supraspinatus) and infraspinous (infraspinatus) fossae; the spine ends in the acromion (articulates with the clavicle; trapezius and deltoid). Teres minor and major near the lateral border. Superior border: scapular notch and coracoid process (pectoralis minor, coracobrachialis, short head of biceps; omohyoid near the notch). Medial border: serratus anterior (front) and rhomboids (back). Angles: superomedial (levator scapulae), inferior (latissimus dorsi), superolateral with the glenoid cavity (humeral head), flanked by the supraglenoid (long head of biceps) and infraglenoid (long head of triceps) tubercles.

Shaft with the radial groove (radial nerve and deep brachial vessels), the deltoid tuberosity ('V' of the deltoid), coracobrachialis medially, triceps lateral head above and medial head below the groove. Proximal end: head (glenoid), anatomical neck, lesser tubercle (subscapularis), greater tubercle (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor from top to bottom), intertubercular (bicipital) groove (long head of biceps), with pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi and teres major inserting around it. Distal end: capitulum (radius), trochlea (ulna), lateral epicondyle (extensors), medial epicondyle (flexors), olecranon fossa behind.

Radius (lateral) and ulna (medial), linked by proximal and distal radio-ulnar joints and the interosseous membrane. Radius: anterior face (flexor pollicis longus, pronator quadratus), lateral face (supinator, pronator teres), posterior face (supinator, abductor and extensor pollicis longus); head (capitulum and ulnar radial notch), neck, radial tuberosity (biceps tendon); distal end articulating with scaphoid and lunate, radial styloid (brachioradialis), ulnar notch. Ulna: olecranon and coronoid process around the trochlear notch, head distally. Hand: 8 carpal bones in two rows (scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform; trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate), 5 metacarpals, 14 phalanges.
